title: Principles over Speed
content:
A team of three university students built a mobile and web application in under 72 hours for a weekend hackathon. Within a month, over a dozen campus organizations adopted the tool, exposing student names, phone numbers, GCash screenshots, ID photos, and private chats to severe vulnerabilities. AI coding assistants were programmed to follow the “make it run” philosophy. As such, it tends to omit implementing features like authorization, access control, and credential isolation unless explicitly told to do so. The team’s prototype violated the following secure design principles.

Grounding the Analysis in Secure Design Principles

Regarding Insecure Direct Object Reference, the vulnerable principles were Least Privilege & Fail-Safe Defaults. The teams blindly trusted user-supplied input in their /profile/{id} route without checking whether the user has read access to the profile document in the database. This insecure design practice is formally known as Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR). A successful IDOR attack could get the attacker access to all users’ private data including group chats and profile pictures. The teams should have implemented an indirect reference, ideally using a JWT-signed session or a server-side session ID, to check whether a user has read access to a particular document or file.

Regarding Hardcoded Secrets in Source Control, the vulnerable principles were Separation of Duties & Complete Mediation. The teams violated the Separation of Duties principle by committing their database and payment credentials in the same repository where the application code resides. Anyone with access to the repository could see the secrets in the plaintext, which should have been strictly prohibited. A proper implementation would have isolated the application code and database schema from the secrets. According to the Complete Mediation principle, the application should have mediated all accesses to the database to verify that it is coming from an authorized source. However, the teams failed to implement this by directly exposing the application's database to the internet.

Regarding Information Disclosure & Over-Privileged Data Access, the vulnerable principles were Least Privilege & Defense in Depth. The teams allowed all users to access all database records, violating the Least Privilege principle. At the same time, the application did not implement proper defense-in-depth to protect sensitive data such as user contact information and student ID pictures. Additionally, the application was disclosing sensitive information such as stack traces when an error occurs. According to the Defense in Depth principle, the teams should have implemented layers of security throughout the architecture so that a single point of failure would not lead to a successful attack.

Regarding Unencrypted Transit and Security Through Obscurity, the vulnerable principles were Open Design & Defense in Depth. The teams used HTTP instead of HTTPS to communicate with the app's users, violating the Open Design principle. The Open Design principle dictates that the security of a system should be based on the openness of its design rather than secrecy. Using HTTP meant that anyone who knows how to use a packet sniffer could intercept and read students' personal information such as ID pictures. Additionally, the teams relied too heavily on the obscurity of their URL routes to secure their application, violating the Defense in Depth principle.

Two-Horizon Remediation

I propose that the teams address this technical debt in two horizons. The first horizon focuses on incident response while the second focuses on retrofitting the application according to secure design principles.

Horizon 1: Incident Response (Hours to Days)

For secret revocation and repository sanitization, the team should revoke and rotate all database and payment credentials in the provider dashboard. This satisfies the Least Privilege principle because revoked credentials can no longer access the production database. For transport layer security, the team should obtain a Let's Encrypt certificate and configure HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS). This satisfies Defense in Depth by adding another layer of encryption to protect sensitive information such as student ID pictures. For error sanitization, the team should implement exception-handling middleware that captures unhandled exceptions internally while displaying a generic message (e.g., "500 Internal Server Error, Reference ID #1042") to end users. This satisfies the Fail-Safe Defaults principle by preventing the disclosure of sensitive debugging information.

Horizon 2: Long-Term Design Retrofitting (Weeks)

For contextual authorization, the team should implement authorization middleware that validates every request before it reaches the application server. This satisfies the Complete Mediation principle. For example, JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) could verify each request before access is granted. To satisfy Fail-Safe Defaults, all database records should be protected behind authorization middleware with role-based access control (RBAC) that explicitly denies unauthorized users. For isolated media storage, media files should be moved into private object storage and accessed through pre-signed URLs. This satisfies Separation of Duties by ensuring files are only accessible to authorized users for a limited time. For secret management and security automation, the team should use a dedicated secret management system and automated security scanners to detect hardcoded credentials during development and deployment. This satisfies the Open Design and Psychological Acceptability principles by reducing reliance on manual code reviews.

Speed, AI Assistants, and Legal Duties Under RA No. 10173

AI coding assistants do not consider legal liability because they are designed to generate working code rather than secure systems. The faculty adviser is correct in stating that the team members who knew about the vulnerabilities may have legal liabilities under Republic Act No. 10173, the Philippine Data Privacy Act of 2012. Based on Section 20 (Privacy by Design), the team should have processed personal data according to the principles of a responsible data controller or processor. They should have implemented appropriate organizational and technical safeguards to protect confidentiality, privacy, and freedom of expression. Consequently, it was their responsibility to protect the prototype against unauthorized access, disclosure, and destruction of student data.

Additionally, Section 21 (Principle of Accountability) states that developers and data controllers remain accountable for the personal data they process. Even if the organizations deploying the prototype were held primarily responsible, the development team and their faculty adviser still had an obligation to recognize these risks and build the prototype according to secure design principles.

Deadlines should never override responsibility. Hackathons encourage a "move fast" philosophy, but functioning software is not necessarily secure software. Developers should always design with security in mind and follow the requirements of Republic Act No. 10173, the Philippine Data Privacy Act of 2012, to ensure privacy and security by design.
